video.title: The #1 Backscratch Mistake — and How to Fix It

classification.reason: The coach provides executable drills and cues, including an isolated forearm rotation drill in front of the body, overhead dry swings, and a self-toss bopping drill directly above the head.

problem.title_as_question: What is the #1 mistake players make in the backscratch position on the serve, and how can it be fixed?
problem.definition: Players mistake the backscratch position for the maximum power position and jackknife the racket straight up toward the ball, skipping the critical outward forearm supination stretch that powers pronation.
problem.target_player: Players who get stuck in the backscratch position or lack explosive power on their serve

symptoms.description: The racket travels straight up toward the ball from the backscratch position rather than continuing to flick outward.
The forearm fails to stretch outward into full supination, remaining truncated at the backscratch position.
Serve lacks explosive power and snap despite the shoulder reaching maximum stretch.
The server feels stuck in the backscratch position or feels like the shoulder is driving the strike instead of the forearm.

causes.statement: Players jackknife the racket straight up toward the ball from the backscratch position rather than throwing it back and out.
The racket does not continue flicking outward into maximum forearm supination stretch before moving up toward the strike.
Players focus on shoulder stretch as the hitting action rather than recognizing forearm pronation as the final link in the kinetic chain.

angles.summary: The shoulder stretch passes energy into the arm, but forearm pronation is the final link in the kinetic chain that actually hits the ball.
Vic Braden's cue: do not scratch your own back (shoulder stretch); scratch your partner's back (full forearm supination stretch).
Medvedev's serve moves mostly straight over the top from backscratch with minimal stretch, contrasting with Sampras, Alcaraz, and Lisicki who flick out into deep supination.
The backscratch position is not the max power position of the serve, but merely an arbitrary dynamic transit point for the forearm.
Visualize the racket oriented horizontally with the racket tip positioned inside your hand prior to the into-out bopping action.

solutions.summary: Explore forearm pronation and supination directly in front of your chest without raising the racket overhead or involving the shoulder.
Take the isolated forearm rotation overhead and practice dry into-out bopping swings with minimal shoulder movement.
Toss the ball directly above your head so it would land on your head or hat, and bop it with isolated forearm pronation toward the baseline.
solutions.external_goal: Bop the ball toward the baseline rather than down into the service box

solutions.summary: Imagine the racket is horizontal with the tip resting well on the inside of your hand before releasing the bopping action.
solutions.external_goal: Racket tip positioned on the inside of the hand

solutions.summary: When moving past the backscratch position, tell yourself to let the forearm roll out rather than trying to back scratch.
